mechanism_fit: This realises R5 (M7, inverse pair) with the ZIP DOS-timestamp encode/decode pair in ZipUtil, reached through an archive write/read round trip. The encoder is ZipUtil.toDosTime(long). It is correct and has a legitimately asymmetric step: it stores getSeconds() >> 1, because DOS time has 2-second resolution and drops odd seconds by design. It also clamps years before 1980 and applies the java.util.Date offsets (+1900, +1). The decoder is ZipUtil.dosToJavaTime, the gold. Its fault is a subtle omission: it no longer multiplies the 5-bit seconds field by 2. Its remaining body reads as complete, in the same style as the other field lines. The trigger writes an entry stamped 10:20:46 with ZipArchiveOutputStream and reads it back with ZipFile. It gets 10:20:23, an exact halving that fits either side: either the encoder should not halve, or the decoder should double. The encoder's visible >> 1 is the asymmetric-looking lure.
gold: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipUtil::dosToJavaTime (src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/zip/ZipUtil.java). The fault changes `cal.set(Calendar.SECOND, (int) (dosTime << 1) & 0x3e);` to `cal.set(Calendar.SECOND, (int) dosTime & 0x1f);`. The minimal repair restores the doubling.
decoys: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipUtil::toDosTime (ZipUtil.java, decl 'long t') - the inverse encoder; it has the legitimately asymmetric seconds>>1 halving
org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipFile::populateFromCentralDirectory (ZipFile.java) - reads the central-directory time word and calls dosToJavaTime
org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipArchiveOutputStream::writeCentralFileHeader (ZipArchiveOutputStream.java) - writes the toDosTime word into the central record
org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipLong::getValue (ZipLong.java, decl 'byte[] bytes, int offset') - little-endian decode of the time word
ownership_reason: ZipUtil.toDosTime packs (year-1980)<<25 | month<<21 | day<<16 | hour<<11 | minute<<5 | getSeconds()>>1. Because the minute field starts at bit 5, the seconds field has only 5 bits (0-31) and has to hold seconds/2. The existing, passing ZipUtilTest.testZipLong rebuilds the same word on its own with cal.get(Calendar.SECOND) >> 1, which pins the encoder's halving. The inverse, dosToJavaTime, is used by ZipFile.populateFromCentralDirectory for every entry and by ZipUtil.fromDosTime, so it has to multiply the field by 2. In the variant it sets Calendar.SECOND from the raw field, so 46 is read back as 23. The writer (writeCentralFileHeader) and the reader (populateFromCentralDirectory, ZipLong.getValue) only move the 4-byte word unchanged. Dropping the encoder's halving instead pushes seconds of 32 or more into the minute field (the trigger then reads 10:21:14) and breaks testZipLong. Restoring the doubling in dosToJavaTime alone makes the trigger and the full suite pass. The ownership test is ZipUtilTest::testZipLong; it passes on both the CORRECT and the variant configuration.
trigger: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.ZipTestCase::testEntryTimestampRoundTrip, a new JUnit3 method in src/test/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/ZipTestCase.java. It builds a local Calendar for 2008-06-15 10:20:46 (cleared, so 0 ms). It writes one entry "stamped.txt" with that time via new ZipArchiveOutputStream(File), reopens the file with new ZipFile(File), and asserts that SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss") of getEntry("stamped.txt").getTime() equals "2008-06-15 10:20:46". Comparing at second resolution keeps it deterministic. Added imports: java.text.SimpleDateFormat, java.util.Calendar, java.util.Date, ZipArchiveOutputStream, ZipFile.
construction_notes: Lang was considered first: StringEscapeUtils escapeJava/unescapeJava with supplementary characters, gold UnicodeEscaper.translate and decoy UnicodeUnescaper.translate. I rejected it because Lang-1f's CharSequenceTranslator.translate(CharSequence, Writer) has a real latent defect: it advances with codePointAt(input, pt) instead of pos (the upstream Lang-6 fix). That defect sits on any supplementary-character trigger path. Leaving it would put a second genuine defect next to the gold; fixing it would need a context edit that is not behaviour-preserving. The other Lang encode/decode pairs (CSV, numeric entities, Conversion, Fraction, FastDate*) had their candidate omissions caught by the existing suites. In Compress-1f the ZIP DOS-time pair is clean. No existing test reads back entry times, so screening the full suite on a /private/tmp copy with the fault applied gave 0 failures (73 tests), and only the new trigger fails. No context edits. Three compensating edits are declared: drop the encoder halving (trigger reads 10:21:14 and testZipLong fails); route the ZipFile reader through ZipUtil.fromDosTime (equivalent, trigger still fails); round the encoder's halved seconds up (trigger still fails). The validator ran once and gave overall READY with every gate passing (G0 to G12, including G6: gold and all 4 decoys executed). concerns: 1) The gold and the main competitor (toDosTime) are in the same ~100-line file, and the bit-width argument (5-bit seconds field) is quick to find. The instance tests attribution between the two inverse sides rather than search, so strong models may hit a ceiling. 2) Pristine upstream quirk inside the gold method: dosToJavaTime never resets Calendar.MILLISECOND, so decoded times carry the current milliseconds. The trigger avoids this by comparing at second resolution. A model may mention it, but because it is in the gold method, method-level ranking is unaffected. 3) A pristine upstream FIXME comment sits next to the dosToJavaTime call in ZipFile.populateFromCentralDirectory. It may pull attention to that decoy, but it is unchanged from upstream. 4) Owner invariance covers only the declared, natural one-line edits. An unnatural call-site hack in ZipFile, such as adding (word & 0x1f) seconds after dosToJavaTime, could make the trigger pass because no existing test checks read-back times. Such a hack would duplicate the conversion and leave the public ZipUtil.fromDosTime wrong. It was not declared. 5) The round trip goes through JDK ZipEntry.setTime/getTime (Java 11, lossless extended DOS time) and the default time zone on both sides. 2008-06-15 10:20:46 avoids DST transitions. 6) The ownership test testZipLong uses new Date(), but it compares two encodings of the same instant, so it passes deterministically.
